1:
Who the descending angel is nobody agrees. Robertson settles only the negative, that he is not the angel of the seventeenth chapter who guided John but one sent to announce the doom of Babylon, and borrows Swete's picture, that so recently has he come from the Presence that in passing he flings a broad belt of light across the dark earth. Wesley notes he is called another with respect to the angel of the tenth chapter, and turns the lustre into an argument: if such is the brightness of the servant, what image could display the majesty of the Lord. Bede allegorises without hesitating, taking the angel for the Lord himself incarnate or else for the doctors of the Church, endued with heavenly light and announcing that the kingdom of heaven is at hand. Clarke reads him as a human messenger of the everlasting gospel who by preaching and writings should diffuse the light of truth. Ellicott declines the identification and asks instead what the light does: it shines like day upon the tawdry splendour of Babylon and shows that what was admired was worthless. Henry observes only that he had light not merely to discern his own prediction but to inform the world, and power as well as light.

The doubled cry is traced by all to Isaiah, and disputed once. Henry reports the opinion that the repetition marks a double fall, first her apostasy and then her ruin, and rejects it: what follows describes not her sin of entertaining idols but her punishment, since unclean spirits and ominous birds were commonly supposed to haunt a city lying in ruins. Robertson calls the repeated aorists a solemn dirge of the damned. On the terms of the desolation there is a quieter division. Barnes and Robertson take the word for hold as watch-post or garrison rather than prison, Robertson adding Swete's image of evil spirits watching over fallen Rome like night-birds that build their eyries in the broken towers; Ellicott renders it prison twice over and turns the verse moral, that her palaces are seen to be prisons, her highest wisdom little more than low cunning, her sweetest songs discordant cries. Gill alone asks why the voice must be loud, and answers that Babylon will be in a deep sleep, insensible of her ruin until it comes upon her.

What Babylon stands for is the open question of the chapter, and each voice answers differently. Clarke lists three readings without choosing, Rome pagan, Rome papal, and Jerusalem. Barnes chooses firmly for the Papacy and then guards the choice, that not the city of Rome itself is meant but the Antichristian power seated there, so that nothing in the chapter need be looked for literally. Wesley argues from the Romanist premise against it, that if Babylon means heathen Rome and that destruction is past, then devils and unclean spirits are its only inhabitants for ever. Gill narrows the drinking nations to those of the Roman empire and of Europe, since the pagan and Mahometan nations have not drunk. Bede looks for no city at all, calling it the city of the devil, and glosses the merchants' enrichment as an infelicitous traffic by which men exchange their souls for temporal abundance, excess of luxuries making poor instead of rich. Ellicott sets the three parties of the verse in order, that she has been an enemy to mankind as nations, kings and merchants together, bringing delirium on the first, reducing the second, bribing the third, and with both hands earnestly has she sinned. Robertson notes the variant between having drunk and having fallen, and that here alone in the New Testament do we catch a glimpse of the vast traffic between east and west that made Rome rich, while Barnes defines the word behind her delicacies as properly rudeness or insolence, and so revel, riot and luxury.
4:
Whose the voice is, and what it commands, are answered with varying confidence. Gill will not choose between another angel, the same angel, and God or Christ himself, though he leans to the last since those addressed are called his people; Wesley says flatly it is Christ, warning a people secretly scattered even there; Barnes thinks it seems rather to be God's voice; Ellicott refuses the question, that a voice of divine love giving warning is enough. On the command Ellicott is most careful: the coming forth is not a bodily exodus from Rome but that separation from the spirit of the world without which we are entangled in its habits, and though the duty may lead to a literal exodus and even to secession from a world-corrupted church, the jeopardy lies in attachment to the world-spirit. Barnes presses harder, that separation was a duty which not only justifies the Reformation but would have made longer continuance in that communion, once its wickedness was seen, an act of guilt. Robertson supplies the pedigree of the summons, the call of Abram and the rescue of Lot behind the prophets; Clarke offers a couplet of Mantuanus instead of an argument, that those who would live godly should depart, since at Rome all things are lawful except to be good.

Over the sins that reach heaven the disagreement is about the image. Ellicott takes it literally as a heap, firmly fastened and towering like another Babel as far as heaven, and says expressly that this is more than the cry of sin reaching heaven as at Sodom, since the sins themselves have touched the face of heaven. Barnes denies exactly that, holding the meaning is not a pile but that the guilt had become prominent enough to attract God's attention, and compares the blood of Abel crying from the ground. Gill and Robertson settle the philology in Ellicott's favour without arguing it, Robertson deriving the verb from the word for glue, Gill reporting the Alexandrian and Complutensian reading which gives cleaved or glued, so that her sins were soldered together and stuck fast to her.

The call for a double recompense is qualified by nearly everyone who touches it. Ellicott corrects the received text twice, that the word rendered you should be omitted, since it is not the saints who repay her, and that the double does not mean double her sins, her sins being themselves called double. Wesley reduces it further, that by Hebrew idiom it implies a full retaliation only. Robertson notes the double recompense was according to the Levitical law, and Barnes leaves both possibilities open, the quantity doubled or the ingredients doubled in intensity. Gill alone names the executioners, the seven angels and the ten kings: as she stripped the saints of their goods she shall be stripped of her attire, and as she burnt many of the precious saints in the flames, as here in England, so shall she be utterly burnt.

The last verse produces the sharpest dissent here. Ellicott arranges the plagues as a fourfold answer, death for her scorn of widowhood, mourning for her revelling, famine for her abundance, fire for her fornication; Wesley makes the same point more briefly, that they fall on the very things from which she imagined herself most safe. Robertson takes the one day as a symbol of suddenness, like the one hour following. Barnes argues at length that the burning may be more than figure and Rome itself literally destroyed by fire, canvassing Jewish and early Christian expectation to that effect. Clarke refuses the whole application: of what city is this spoken, he asks, since Rome pagan was never so treated, Alaric and Totilas having burnt only parts of it, and Rome papal has not been so treated either, whereas it is true of Jerusalem, which is not generally thought to be intended.
9:
Henry sorts the mourners first. The kings were flattered into idolatry by being allowed to be arbitrary and tyrannical over their subjects so long as they were obsequious; the merchants trafficked for indulgences, pardons and preferments, and mourn because by that craft they got their wealth. His decisive point concerns the cause of the mourning: it was not their sin but their punishment, since they lament not their fall into idolatry and luxury and persecution but their fall into ruin, the spirit of antichrist being a worldly spirit and their sorrow a worldly sorrow. Ellicott reaches the same verdict another way, that the grief is fear mingled with selfishness, the mourners remembering with a regret only tempered by terror the voluptuous life they have lost. Barnes turns the verse political instead, holding that the kings of Europe owed much of their influence to Papal support, that Europe might long since have been free without it, and that the fall of this power will be the signal for a general overturning of its thrones. Clarke says only that these are the kings who copied her superstitions.

That they stand at a distance is agreed, and explained four ways: Henry makes it a moral: even Babylon's friends stand at a distance from her fall, willing to share her pleasures but not her plagues. Barnes reads it as impotence, that those who so long sustained the Papal power will not even attempt to rescue it. Clarke has them beholding her desolations with astonishment, utterly unable to afford assistance. Gill offers both causes without choosing, that either they are in no capacity to help or they are dispirited and in awe of God's judgments. Robertson alone describes fascination rather than fear, that there is a weird charm in a burning city, and compares Nero's delight in the burning of Rome; they are held by the lurid blaze and yet afraid to draw near. Ellicott stands back to describe the architecture of the laments: kings, merchants and shippers each take their turn, each stands afar off, each begins with an Alas, and the words in one hour recur at the close of every dirge with the monotony of a passing bell heard at intervals amid the strains of sad music. Wesley contributes a philological aside, that Rome was anciently termed by its inhabitants Valentia, that is strong, and that the name Rome itself signifies strength in Greek.

The catalogue of merchandise raises a question about how the vision is to be read, and Gill puts it sharply. The list cannot be understood merely literally, he argues, because such commodities, if they do not sell at one place, will sell at another; the decline of trade in one city does not stop business the world over, and often the ruin of commerce in one place is the rise of it in another, so that all these things but the last will be merchandised somewhere to the end of the world. Nor will it help to restrict the loss to Rome and its neighbourhood, since goods unsold there could be sold elsewhere and would not warrant so great a lamentation. Barnes treats the enumeration far more lightly, as inserted to fill out the picture of such a city and show the desolation when its traffic is suspended. Robertson takes it as documentary, glossing the word for cargo as a ship's lading, counting twenty-nine items of import into the port of Rome, citing Galen and Pliny and Aristides on the commerce that made Rome the world's chief market, and noting how closely the items follow the destruction of Tyre in Ezekiel. Clarke abandons comment altogether and prints instead a long paraphrase of Bishop Bale, in which her mitred merchants and soul-sellers wax rich through the sale of oils, cream, salt, water, bread, orders, hallowings, ashes, palm, wax, beads, crosses, bells, organs, images, relics and other pedlary wares.
12:
Whether the cargo is Roman trade or an allegory of church wares divides the voices. Robertson treats it as documentary and glosses item by item: the silk takes its name from the people from whom the fabric came after Alexander invaded India, the thyine is a North African citrus prized for a grain like a peacock's tail, the cinnamon Phoenician as to name and possibly South Chinese as to origin. Barnes runs the same course with Gibbon at his elbow, that pearls claimed first rank after the diamond among the luxuries of Rome and that a variety of aromatics was consumed in religious worship and the pomp of funerals. Gill runs two readings at once. Literally the merchandise is the riches which cardinals, bishops, monks and friars bring into their coffers and the pope's by trading in the souls of men, Brightman adding that Spain fetches these wares from the Indies for Rome. Mystically the gold and silver are the doctrines of the gospel, which Rome's merchants pretended to deliver out while putting off wood and hay and stubble instead; and the cinnamon, used by harlots to perfume their bed, he refers to the licensed brothels of Rome. Clarke abandons his own comment a second time for another stretch of Bishop Bale, itemising the pontifical rings and censers and two-horned mitres which men who know the word of God will no longer pay for.

The last two items produce the sharpest disagreement. Robertson insists the word rendered slaves is simply bodies, treated as animals or implements alongside the horses and chariots, cites the usage from Genesis, Tobit and Maccabees, calls the traffic human live stock after Swete, and notes that the slave merchant was named a body-merchant; he then suggests the following conjunction should be rendered not and but even, so that bodies and souls of men are one article and not two. Barnes reports Stuart's narrower construction, that the word means grooms, a class of slaves employed about horses and carriages. Wesley keeps the phrases apart and makes the second the worse, that souls of men are continually bought and sold at Rome and that this is the most gainful merchandise of all there; he also notices that the word for chariots is purely Latin inserted into the Greek, which he thinks John used on purpose. Cyril is not commenting on the cargo but on the two comings of Christ, quoting Malachi that the Lord shall come as a refiner's fire and be a swift witness against the sorcerers and adulteresses; yet the passage he reaches for next lands on the same materials, that whoever builds gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay or stubble shall have his work made manifest, because the day shall declare it and it shall be revealed in fire.

With the fruits the description breaks into address. Ellicott marks the change, that the description is interrupted and Babylon herself spoken to, which suits the fervour of the chapter, and he presses the tense, that the word means these things departed once for all rather than are departed, closing with the judgment that the desire of the wicked has perished. Robertson calls the same form a prophetic aorist and separates the adjectives that follow, one from a word for grease and used of food, the other bright and shining and used of clothing. Barnes takes the noun from the season, the dog-days when Sirius is predominant and the fruits ripen, and Clarke says the same in a line. Wesley alone insists the turn is domestic, that the vision passes from imports to the home delicacies of Rome, the word covering pears, peaches, nectarines and all of the apple and plum kinds. Gill takes it mystically once more, that the fruits are the universal dominion and the obedience of kings, of which a large harvest was expected and which is now at an end.
15:
The merchants' dirge opens a dispute about whether the finery is worn or sold. Barnes takes the city as personified, so that what were articles of traffic now clothe her as a woman dressed in the richest of them. Clarke denies it on lexical grounds, that the verb rendered clothed often signifies to abound or be laden with, as Kypke shows from the best Greek writers, and that these are not personal ornaments but the articles of trade in which the city trafficked. Gill notes only that the merchants use the same words as the kings, and Robertson marks the structure, that this is the dirge of the merchants as the earlier was the dirge of the kings.

The hour raises a question of consistency, and Barnes answers it: her plagues were said earlier to come in one day and here so great riches comes to nothing in one hour, but the shorter term is what the ruin seemed to the lookers-on. He then finds a textual difficulty in the same verse, the received reading giving the whole company in ships where the editors he follows give one who sails to a place, a coaster who does not venture far out to sea. Clarke prefers that reading and explains the practice behind it: it marks the traffic of the Mediterranean coast, where in those times, the compass being unknown, every voyage was performed within sight of land. Robertson keeps to the ranks aboard, that the shipmaster is the helmsman and subordinate to the supreme commander, and that the mariners work the sea in an idiom as old as Hesiod. Gill supplies a proverb, that the Jews said if ten measures of riches descended into the world the ancient Romans took nine. When the smoke is seen Robertson lets one sentence carry the verse, that the eternal city is eternal no longer.

The mourning gestures are traced to their source. Wesley states the principle plainly, that most of the expressions describing this downfall are taken from Ezekiel's description of the downfall of Tyre. Ellicott glosses her costliness as her extravagances of living and the splendour of palaces that drew their materials from all ports, and observes that this third lament ends as the others did with the tolling of the one hour. Barnes and Clarke agree that the dust on the head is the ordinary sign of grief, Clarke adding that here no sorrow is dissembled.

The summons to rejoice is guarded by nearly everyone. Barnes insists it is not the language of vengeance but of exultation that the cause of truth may now spread without hindrance, and prefers the reading which sets a conjunction between the saints and the apostles, so that three classes are addressed rather than two. Gill canvasses four senses of heaven without settling on one: the heavens themselves, the angels, whom the Syriac names outright, the souls under the altar who have long cried for vengeance, or the true church on earth, which this book often calls heaven. Ellicott corrects the phrase about judgment, that your judgment is judged on her means not a judgment the saints decreed but the judgment Babylon wrought on the holy now exacted from her; and he meets an argument nobody else raises, that because the verse names apostles in heaven some have inferred the twelve were all dead before the Apocalypse was written and therefore John did not write it, to which he answers that the verse states nothing about who has passed into heaven. Robertson finds the sharpest contrast, that the verb here for rejoicing is the one used earlier of the joy of the wicked over the death of the two witnesses, and that the word for judgment means a case brought to trial rather than a sentence. Henry gives the local sting, that the apostles idolatrously worshipped at Rome will rejoice in her fall.
21:
The millstone is read as a sign, and its physics noticed. Ellicott traces the image to Jeremiah, where Seraiah was told to bind the prophetic roll to a great stone and cast both into the Euphrates, and reads the dead mass sinking by the law of its own weight as a fall past recovery; he renders the adverb with a bound, and closes the antithesis himself, that she who sat as a queen upon many waters sinks as a stone in the mighty waters. Robertson insists on the size, not the small millstone turned by women but one requiring an ass, a boulder hurled into the sea. Clarke attends to the mechanics, that the stone falls with the accelerated force of gravitation and with that force increased by the projectile force the destroying angel impresses on it. Who the angel is they differ over: Gill will have him neither Christ nor a ministering spirit but some man or set of men, Barnes an angel distinct from the one at the head of the chapter.

Both Ellicott and Robertson count the refrain, the one finding the words no more repeated six times like a funeral knell over departed greatness, the other counting the same negatives grammatically as a fourfold sonorous repetition with two more following. Wesley alone reads the silences as a social ladder: music was the entertainment of the rich, trade the business of the middle rank, bread-making the employment of the lowest, and marriages the means by which cities are peopled, so that no rank could live there any more, nor would it be repeopled. Barnes takes the list as representative, only the principal instruments named for the rest. Gill presses the candle into a retribution: where wax candles burned in daylight there will not be one to give light at night, and where candles were lighted for the dead there will not be one for the living.

On the sorceries the comment turns modern: Ellicott first removes a misreading, that the judgment falls not because her merchants were great men but for the sorcery of the next clause, which he glosses as her artful policy and the seductions by which she drew the nations into the meshes of her worldliness. Wesley says the same of the merchants, that their greatness was in itself indifferent and yet led them into pride and luxury. Robertson takes the Greek word toward its English descendant and asks how medicine came to be bound up with sorcery, answering from the present: quackery in patent medicines, witch-doctors, professional faith-healers, true medical science having had a hard fight to shake off charlatanry, and such charlatans always finding victims.

The blood at the end divides them furthest. Barnes takes the charge nearly at face value, that persecution there was so constant that all the blood ever shed may be said to have been poured out there. Ellicott denies the literal sense expressly: it is not meant that all the blood shed by violence had been shed by Rome or any single city, but that the world city is founded on principles whose logical outcome is violence, so that those who die by her hands, few or many, are evidence of the tendency of her power; and he draws the rule that in the earthly view we are guilty of the acts we do, in the heavenly view of all that the spirit of our conduct tends to do. Wesley piles up numbers instead, the boast of Charles the Ninth that he had destroyed seventy thousand Huguenots and the computation that fifteen millions of Protestants perished by the Inquisition in thirty years, though he grants it may be overcharged. Robertson borrows Dill's phrase, that Rome butchered to make a Roman holiday. Clarke, having refused the application once, refuses it again: no city is yet answerable to all these things, and the prophecy must remain to be fulfilled.
